newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - 5-yr note sale to weigh on mkt. [CORRECTED 23:38 GMT]
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - 5-yr note sale to weigh on mkt. [CORRECTED 23:38 GMT]

text.p: U.S. bond market participants said they expected Treasuries to remain under pressure on Thursday, as supply concerns continue to weigh on the market.

The Treasury is slated to sell $12.5 billion five-year notes Thursday afternoon. Players said it is a good bet the market will try and cheapen the issue up ahead of the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline.
Late Wednesday, the when-issued five-year note was at 6.32 percent (corrects rate from 5.32 percent).

"There is not going to be enough interest in five-years" at 6.32 percent, said Michael McClure, head trader at Zions First National Bank, adding that the market will likely to try to push the issue up to at least the mid-6.30 (corrects from "mid-5.30") percent range.
The five-year auction follows a fairly good two-year note sale on Wednesday. But lack of follow-through pushed the two-year from its issued rate of 5.984 percent to 6.01 by late afternoon.
"I don't think the five-year can perform as poorly as the two-year," McClure said, noting the issue is about 10 basis points from its recent lows.
The poor post-auction action led to a decline in Treasury prices, which had been mostly unchanged before the auction. The 30-year bond was at 95-27/32, down a half-point, to yield 6.83 percent.

Ahead of the five-year note auction, the Labor Department will release weekly jobless claims figures at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Claims are seen at 347,000 in the week ended January 18, up from 323,000 the prior week, according to a Reuters poll.
At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, import/export prices for December are due, with analysts predicting a 0.4 percent rise in import prices, after a 0.1 percent decline in November.
But unless far from expectations, market participants don't expect the data to affect trading so much.
"The market is waiting for the ECI," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney Inc, referring to Tuesday's long-awaited employment cost index report for the fourth-quarter.

Held and others said the market is still nervous that wage pressures will eventually show up in consumer prices. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan said on Tuesday he was watching that closely. A host of other Fed officials echoed those thoughts in recent days and weeks.
And, the Fed's Beige Book, released Wednesday afternoon, noted some signs of wage pressures, but price pressures were "moderate overall."
Nevertheless, players said the Fed should leave official interest rates steady until late March at the earliest.

Late Wednesday, the outstanding two-year note was down 2/32 at 99-18/32 to yield 5.99 percent. The 10-year note was at 99-20/32, down 9/32, to yield 6.55 percent. Bill rates ended unchanged to two basis points higher.
